bridges.description: Show that the universe’s existence and finite beginning require an external personal cause.
Show that cosmic fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than necessity or chance.
Connect objective moral value to an essentially good divine foundation.
Use the resurrection hypothesis and its historical grounds as evidence for God.
Defend immediate experience of God as a possible source of knowledge beyond public arguments.
Establish that the cumulative pro case makes God’s existence more plausible than atheism.
Compare what the world would probably be like under theism and atheism using observed evidence.
Argue that widespread reasonable nonbelief is unexpected if a loving God seeks relationship.
Argue that scientific success, embodied minds, and evolutionary history fit atheism better than theism.
Argue that apparently pointless suffering and lack of divine reassurance count against a perfectly good God.
Challenge the explanatory and evidential links in the cosmological, moral, resurrection, and experiential cases.
Establish that the total evidence makes atheism more reasonable than theism.

sections.title: Cosmic existence and origin
sections.rationale: The contingency and beginning arguments supply a direct route from the universe to a transcendent personal cause.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and evolutionary design
sections.rationale: Competing expectations about cosmic parameters and biological history bear centrally on intelligent design.

sections.title: Moral reality and suffering
sections.rationale: The exchange tests both a moral-ground argument for God and suffering as evidence against perfect goodness.

sections.title: Divine hiddenness and relationship
sections.rationale: This exchange tests whether a loving God’s desire for relationship predicts clearer disclosure to reasonable nonbelievers.

sections.title: Scientific explanation and divine action
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute whether science’s lawfulness and lack of invoked divine actions favor either worldview.

sections.title: Minds, brains, and personhood
sections.rationale: The status of human minds bears on whether immaterial agency is coherent and expected under either worldview.

sections.title: Resurrection and religious experience
sections.rationale: Historical and experiential claims are Craig’s principal bridges from generic theism to Christian theism and personal warrant.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The universe requires an explanation outside itself, plausibly a transcendent personal cause.
moves.warrant: Anything that exists has its explanation either in its own necessary nature or in an external cause; the universe exists, and a nonphysical cause cannot be an inert abstract object.
moves.inference: Because the universe is not self-explanatory and abstract objects cannot cause, its explanation is an intelligent mind beyond space and time.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the complete explanatory-principle argument, its necessary/external distinction, and the personal-cause conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: anything that exists has an explanation of its existence
abstract objects can't cause anything
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: Directly supplies an explanatory route to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: States the contingency-style foundation and its personal-cause bridge.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent personal creator.
moves.warrant: Craig presents Big Bang cosmology as evidence that matter, space, and time began, adds the causal premise, and argues that a timeless sufficient cause of a temporal effect must act personally.
moves.inference: A caused beginning of spacetime points beyond physical reality to a powerful agent who freely creates.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the complete second argument from its announced premise through the personal-creator conclusion; disputed numerical details are not used.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: everything that comes into being has a cause
therefore the universe has a cause
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A principal direct argument for a creator.

burdenContact.rationale: Advances the finite-origin branch of the explanatory case.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Life-permitting fine-tuning is best explained by design.
moves.warrant: Physical constants and initial quantities allegedly occupy an extremely narrow life-permitting range, while necessity and chance are said not to account for that range.
moves.inference: If necessity and chance fail, design remains the best of the proposed explanations.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the two kinds of fine-tuning, the three-way explanatory comparison, and the design conclusion while avoiding reliance on disputed exact numbers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: either physical necessity, chance, or design
therefore, it is due to design
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A major independent line in the cumulative pro case.

burdenContact.rationale: States the design inference from cosmic fine-tuning.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Objective moral values exist and require God as their ground.
moves.warrant: Craig distinguishes moral knowledge from moral ontology, argues evolution alone would yield adaptive attitudes rather than objective duties, and appeals to evident cases of genuine wrongness.
moves.inference: If objective values would not exist without God yet do exist, God exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains both premises, the clarification about unbelievers’ moral knowledge, examples, and the stated conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if God does not exist, objective moral values do not exist
objective values do exist
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A direct deductive route to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies the grounding premise and existence premise.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: God’s raising Jesus is the best explanation of the empty tomb, appearances, and disciples’ resurrection belief.
moves.warrant: Craig presents the three items as widely accepted historical facts and rejects familiar naturalistic alternatives as implausible.
moves.inference: If divine resurrection best explains these facts and entails God’s existence, the facts provide inductive evidence for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the full historical case, the three alleged facts, comparison with alternatives, and the explicit four-step inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are three established facts about Jesus
God raised Jesus from the dead is the best explanation
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: Craig’s principal specifically Christian public-evidence argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects the historical hypothesis to God’s existence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: A person may know God directly through immediate experience apart from argument.
moves.warrant: Biblical religious experience is described as encounter with an active reality, and sincere seekers are promised an inward awareness of God.
moves.inference: Immediate experience can provide personal warrant even when public proofs are disputed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Craig’s explicit classification of the claim and his account of immediate experiential warrant.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments
God becomes an immediate reality in their lives
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A distinct subsidiary source of warrant, though Craig says it is not an argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly states the experiential-warrant route.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Widespread reasonable nonbelief is unlikely if a loving God seeks relationship with every capable person.
moves.warrant: Such a God could provide persuasive public or inward evidence, yet many sincere seekers and adherents of nonmonotheistic traditions remain unconvinced.
moves.inference: Divine hiddenness fits atheism better than relational theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the relational expectation, evidence of nonbelief, proposed disclosure mechanisms, and comparative conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is such a thing as reasonable unbelief
The hiddenness of God is highly unlikely given theism
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Dacey’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A central positive evidential argument for atheism.

burdenContact.rationale: Links nonbelief to expectations generated by divine love.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: The success of science without invoking divine action favors atheism.
moves.warrant: Natural sciences explain and predict phenomena through natural causes, whereas an active relational creator would be expected to leave causal actions that scientific history must register.
moves.inference: Science’s ability to ignore God while explaining much is less surprising on atheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the contrast between natural and divine causes, the record of scientific success, and the comparative likelihood inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: science can ignore God and still explain so much
favors atheism over theism
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Dacey’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: An independent comparative line within Dacey’s cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: Uses scientific explanatory practice as comparative evidence.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Human mentality’s dependence on brains is more expected on atheism than on theism.
moves.warrant: The interaction of a nonphysical soul with a body is obscure, while localized abilities, brain injury, and genetic effects closely correlate mental life with physical systems.
moves.inference: Evidence against independent human souls lowers a theistic expectation of immaterial minds more than atheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains both objections to substance dualism, empirical examples, and the comparative theism-atheism conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: highly specific correlations between mental phenomena and brain activity
supports atheism over theism
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Dacey’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A distinct positive evidential comparison about minds.

burdenContact.rationale: Argues embodied mentality fits atheism better.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Wasteful, imperfect evolutionary history is less expected under an all-powerful rational designer.
moves.warrant: Natural selection works through many discarded variants and leaves dysfunctional structures and extensive extinction, unlike purposive advance design.
moves.inference: Those features fit a blind limited mechanism better than divine design.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the mechanism, concrete imperfection examples, extinction, and explicit likelihood comparison.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: The evolutionary process is massively wasteful and inefficient
more likely on the assumption that it is a blind
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Dacey’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A major positive evidential argument against providential design.

burdenContact.rationale: Compares evolutionary history under blind and intelligent processes.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Severe apparently pointless suffering is evidence against a perfectly good, powerful God.
moves.warrant: Preventable child suffering lacks an evident justifying good, and a loving God would provide reasons or reassurance to sufferers if such reasons existed.
moves.inference: Careful failure to find justification, together with experienced abandonment, makes a perfectly good God less probable.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the concrete suffering case, required moral justification, candidate goods, the finite-knower reply, and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: his reason must be such that it morally justifies
we can reasonably conclude that there is no such state
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Dacey’s named opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: A central direct evidential argument against perfect theism.

burdenContact.rationale: States the suffering and absent-reassurance inference.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Hiddenness does not count strongly against God because sufficient evidence may already exist and clearer disclosure need not advance God’s relational aim.
moves.warrant: Craig’s cumulative evidence is offered as ample disclosure; omniscience would identify the form of revelation most effective for freely formed saving relationships, and spectacular proof alone might not foster love.
moves.inference: Dacey must show that clearer revelation would probably produce more saving relationships, not merely more assent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Craig’s three connected hiddenness replies: existing evidence, relational purpose, and claimed inward drawing.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: would not necessarily guarantee that more people would enter
not just to convince them that he exists
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: The principal pro response to a central con argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Attempts to neutralize hiddenness within the overall comparison.

responseComponents.description: Challenges both the claim that evidence is insufficient and the inference from clearer evidence to loving relationship.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Scientific success is compatible with and expected under theism, while miracles remain possible.
moves.warrant: A rational law-governed creation supports scientific inquiry, and historical interventions such as the resurrection would be exceptions rather than replacements for natural law.
moves.inference: Natural science’s success does not favor atheism merely because its ordinary explanations use natural causes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains both of Craig’s announced responses to the science argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it is theism that guarantees the success of natural science
God has periodically intervened in the natural process
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: Directly contests an independent con evidential line.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends theism’s comparative fit with science.

responseComponents.description: Counters the expectation that scientific success and theism conflict.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Brain-mind correlations do not disprove an immaterial, causally effective self.
moves.warrant: Interactionist dualism permits correlations, while first-person identity, intentionality, and agency are said not to reduce to physical properties; Christianity also need not universally require human dualism.
moves.inference: Embodied mental correlations do not by themselves make atheism more likely.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the correlation reply, positive self-acquaintance case, and qualification about Christian materialism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Mere correlations doesn't disprove the reality of the mind
we know ourselves as immaterial persons
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: Directly answers Dacey’s mind-brain evidence and its theological implication.

burdenContact.rationale: Attempts to remove mind-brain evidence from the con cumulative case.

responseComponents.description: Argues the observed correlations remain compatible with interactionist dualism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Evolutionary inefficiency does not count against an unlimited God, and highly improbable macroevolution could instead suggest design.
moves.warrant: Efficiency constrains agents with limited time or resources, neither of which applies to God; Craig also disputes unguided macroevolution by citing alleged improbability.
moves.inference: Evolution is compatible with divine choice and, if extremely improbable unguided, may support intelligence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Craig’s two expressly numbered replies while treating disputed numerical strings only as an unverified general improbability claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: efficiency is important only for a person who has
If God chooses to create via evolution
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: Direct response to Dacey’s evolutionary-design evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends compatibility of design with evolutionary means.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the divine relevance of efficiency and reinterprets improbability as possible design evidence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Humans are poorly placed to judge suffering pointless, and God need not disclose each specific justification.
moves.warrant: Limited temporal and spatial perspective may hide remote goods; general scriptural assurance can guide trust, while specific disclosure might be ineffective or alter the actions needed for the good.
moves.inference: Failure to see a sufficient reason does not make it probable that none exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the epistemic-limitation response, Dacey’s reassurance objection, Craig’s three disclosure replies, and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we're simply not in a good position
doesn't mean that there isn't a reason
moves.attributionRationale: Wholly inside Craig’s named first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: Craig’s main response to the central suffering argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Seeks to prevent suffering from defeating the cumulative pro case.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference from no known justification or reassurance to no divine justification.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Current cosmology does not establish an absolute beginning from nothing.
moves.warrant: The Big Bang theory traces early cosmic evolution but current theory breaks down near time zero, with quantum gravity and origins unresolved.
moves.inference: Using an unsettled scientific frontier as a premise for a theological conclusion is premature.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes the quoted distinction between evolution and origin, current theoretical limits, and Dacey’s conclusion.

moves.importanceRationale: Targets a central empirical premise of Craig’s beginning argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges the scientific bridge from cosmology to absolute beginning.

responseComponents.description: Disputes that Big Bang theory establishes creation from nothing.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Fine-tuning supports theism only if deeper natural laws cannot explain the constants, which remains unknown.
moves.warrant: Physicists do not yet know whether apparent constants are brute facts or consequences of a deeper theory, and past apparent design has received natural explanation.
moves.inference: The exclusion of naturalistic explanations and resulting design inference are premature.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains the conditional challenge, expert uncertainty, historical analogy, and stated naturalistic possibility.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: A timeless personal creator does not yet explain cosmic origins because its mode of causation is obscure.
moves.warrant: Known persons act in time and known creation rearranges material, whereas the proposed cause acts timelessly and creates without material.
moves.inference: Without even a rough mechanism, positing divine causation may label rather than reduce the mystery.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Isolates the complete critique of timeless creation and its explanatory demand.

Challenges timeless personal causation and creation from nothing.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Objective moral worth can rest on morally relevant features of persons rather than God.
moves.warrant: If God cannot arbitrarily assign value, he must recognize features such as suffering, interests, plans, or promises that persons possess independently of divine decision.
moves.inference: Those features can ground value directly, so objective value does not entail God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the divine-decision dilemma, proposed natural features, and explicit conclusion.

moves.warrant: Moving the body to a common grave is offered as a mundane possibility, while the appearances and disciples’ belief are said to lack independent corroboration and arise from partisan later texts.
moves.inference: The alleged facts or their miraculous explanation are insufficiently established to support God’s existence.

moves.speaker: Austin Dacey
moves.claim: Religious experience has not been shown to be a veridical perception of God.

moves.inference: The occurrence of religious experience alone does not establish its divine object.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig

moves.warrant: Craig cites authorities for spacetime’s beginning and contrasts a productive cause with an uncaused origin; causes and effects need not always be temporally separated.
moves.inference: A transcendent productive cause is more plausible than an uncaused emergence and need not precede time.

moves.claim: A deeper physical theory is unlikely to eliminate all fine-tuned parameters.
moves.warrant: Craig cites philosophical and string-theory considerations suggesting later theories will retain numerous constrained values.
moves.inference: The present fine-tuning inference cannot be dismissed merely by hoping for a final theory.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains Craig’s complete answer to the deeper-law objection and his restatement of intelligence as explanation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The moved-body and hallucination proposals do not adequately explain the resurrection evidence.
